 The price of Black Friday

 Black Friday has long signified the kickoff of the holiday shopping season, with stores promising unbeatable deals and almost impossible once-per-year savings. Historically, shoppers have woken up before dawn to wait in long lines, fight crowds and practically swim upstream in a river of people, all trying to score the best bargain. 
 But behind the excitement of these doorbuster sales is a culture of overconsumption. What is marketed as an opportunity to save money has become a major driver of unnecessary spending and environmental waste. 
 Retailers capitalize on consumer psychology by creating a sense of urgency through limited-time offers and countdowns. Shoppers feel like they have to act quickly or they might miss out on the deal. This fear of missing out can lead consumers to purchase goods simply because they are discounted, rather than because they actually need or want them. 
 Some sales might not even be real. A study by the UK consumer group Which? tracked 175 to 201 items across major retailers and discovered that 83% to 99% of the products promoted as Black Friday deals had been sold for the same price or lower at other times of the year. WalletHub, a U.S. personal finance company, found in a 2025 study that 36% of Black Friday listings will offer no savings compared to prices earlier in the year. 
 But misleading discounts are only one part of the problem. Online shopping and cyber deals made the cycle of overconsumption even easier. Gone are the days where you had to leave the comfort of your couch or even get dressed to participate in Black Friday. Now deals on an endless array of items you never really needed are just an internet connection and a click away.  
 Black Friday doesn’t just attack your wallet. The most overlooked impacts of Black Friday are the widespread environmental costs. The increased demand encourages companies to produce more, which on the back end leads to consumption of additional raw materials, water and energy. Online shopping also generates large amounts of cardboard, plastic, bubble wrap and other packaging waste. According to Inside Climate News, as many as 80% of Black Friday purchases along with their plastic packaging end up in landfills or are burned in incinerators. The article also reports that household goods and services are responsible for a little over half of global emissions and the plastic waste from consumer goods is the primary source of physical waste. 
 The good news is you don’t have to fall for the hype of the season. You have the power to push back against Black Friday overconsumption by being more intentional about what you buy. As someone who regularly partakes in retail therapy, I understand the desire to shop and getting caught up in the excitement, only to end up buying things you never really needed.  
 Before you start shopping, make a realistic list of items that you actually need and set a budget to avoid the impulse purchases. Take the time to compare prices and ask yourself whether a sale is truly a good deal or simply a tactic by companies to get you to spend money.  
 This holiday season, let’s choose to be mindful instead of giving in to mindless overconsumption, protecting your hard earned savings and the environment.  
 - Leah Goodwin, business manager
